meta.title: jpm: a fast, small, secure-by-default package manager for JavaScript
meta.description: jpm installs npm packages fast, from one ~2 MB binary, with dependencies' install scripts off and new versions held back a day by default. A drop-in for npm, pnpm, yarn and bun projects.

speed.title: Fast where your CI spends its time
speed.lead: Three real projects, four install phases, eight package managers, against the live npm registry. On GitHub CI jpm is the fastest in 9 of 12 cells; the other three are shown as measured.
speed.phaseDesc.cold: No cache, no lockfile, no node_modules.
speed.phaseDesc.warm: Cache and lockfile kept, node_modules deleted: CI with its cache restored.
speed.phaseDesc.ci: Lockfile kept, no cache, no node_modules: CI with no cache.
speed.phaseDesc.repeat: Nothing changed since the last install.
speed.noRepeat: Repeat installs were not measured on Windows.

speed.windowsNote: Defender scans every file an install writes, and it scans files written by node.exe (npm, upm) far more cheaply than files written by native tools like jpm, aube and pnpm. On Windows jpm is the fastest on next, not yet on nuxt.

lean.title: Small enough to forget it's there
lean.lead: One binary with nothing behind it, an install that holds little in memory, and a store that keeps each file once.

lean.cache: CI cache after a cold next install

storage.title: Each file stored once. Each package built once.
storage.lead: jpm keeps one store per machine and builds each package's directory once, for every project that uses it. Installing again is mostly making links.
storage.step1.title: A content-addressed store
storage.step1.body: Each tarball is checked against its integrity, then unpacked once into ~/.jpm/store. Every file is kept once, by its hash, read-only.
storage.step2.title: A global virtual store
storage.step2.body: Each package is built once as an entry: name@version, plus a short digest of its dependency graph when it has dependencies. Its files are hardlinked from the store, and its dependencies are linked beside it, so it can import only what it declared.
storage.step3.title: Your node_modules
storage.step3.body: A project's node_modules links to those entries. A warm install makes only these few links: 4 ms for nitro on GitHub CI.
storage.step4.title: Every other project
storage.step4.body: The next project on the machine links to the same entries. When nothing changed, a repeat install checks a few links and is done in 1–2 ms.
storage.diagramLabel: Files in the content-addressed store are hardlinked into entries in the global virtual store; each entry links its dependencies beside it, and two projects' node_modules link to the same entries.
storage.perProject.title: Next.js and Nuxt: inside the project
storage.perProject.body: Next's Turbopack compiles nothing outside the project, and Nuxt imports packages it doesn't declare. For a project that depends on next or nuxt, jpm builds the entries in node_modules/.jpm instead, still hardlinked from the store.
security.title: Secure by default
security.lead: The safe setting is the one you get without asking. Loosening one is your call, made in your own settings, not a package's or a cloned repository's.
security.scripts.title: Install scripts wait for you
security.scripts.body: A dependency's install scripts, the way most npm malware runs, don't run until you jpm approve that package and version. A new version waits for approval again.
security.age.title: New versions wait a day
security.age.body: A version published in the last day isn't picked (min-release-age), even when a package deep in the tree pins it exactly, so a hijacked release can't ride in on a pin.
security.exotic.title: No surprise sources
security.exotic.body: A published package can't pull in git or tarball dependencies, or paths outside itself. Only your project and its workspaces choose where code comes from.
security.integrity.title: Checked before it's visible
security.integrity.body: Every package is checked against its lockfile integrity before any of its files are visible to your project.
security.creds.title: No secrets in the lockfile
security.creds.body: Credentials never land in jpm.lock: tokens stay in your .npmrc, and a git URL carrying a password is refused.
security.npmrc.title: A cloned repo can't lower the bar
security.npmrc.body: A project's own .npmrc can't turn off TLS checks, swap the CA or proxy, or loosen the release age. jpm ignores those there and names them in a warning.
security.tls.title: Its own TLS, no OpenSSL
security.tls.body: jpm speaks TLS with its own code, tested against Project Wycheproof and the RFCs' vectors, and checks certificates against Mozilla's roots and your system's.
security.runtimes.title: Runtimes checked by signature
security.runtimes.body: A Node.js runtime a package asks for is checked against the release's SHASUMS256.txt, trusted only once its signature matches Node's release keys.
security.small.title: Less to attack
security.small.body: One ~2 MB binary, with no runtime and no dependency tree of its own to install: less code between you and the registry.
security.note: Secure by default isn't a sandbox: a script you approve runs as you. The details: {scripts} and {config}.
switch.title: Switch in one command
switch.lead: Run jpm install in your project. jpm imports the lockfile you have into its own jpm.lock, with the same versions.
switch.carried: package-lock.json and npm-shrinkwrap.json (npm 7+), pnpm-lock.yaml (pnpm 9+) and bun.lock are carried over as they are: the same versions and the same tree, with no registry lookups.
switch.yarn: yarn.lock, from yarn 1 or yarn 2 and later, keeps every version yarn picked. jpm asks the registry only for what yarn.lock doesn't record: peers, platforms and bins.
switch.untouched: Your old lockfile is left untouched. Delete it when you're ready.
switch.ci: CI keeps working during the switch: jpm ci and jpm install --frozen-lockfile install from the old lockfile as it is until jpm.lock is committed.
switch.setup: It also reads workspaces, pnpm-workspace.yaml, catalogs, overrides and resolutions, and patches.
switch.cmd: reads package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml / yarn.lock / bun.lock → writes jpm.lock
switch.diagramLabel: The lockfiles of npm, pnpm, yarn and bun all become one jpm.lock with the same versions.
switch.more: Older formats, out-of-date lockfiles and the rest: {link}.
story.title: Written by Claude Code. Checked by everyone else's tests.
story.p1: It started with an episode of the Syntax podcast that held up upm as faster and smaller than the rest. Small, because it runs on Node.js. So: what if it were ported to Rust and made small for real? And what would it take to turn an AI's one-shot into something you'd trust in CI?
story.p2: Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5, wrote every line, its own TLS and crypto included. JT Turner, an engineer of 27 years, made the calls. When Claude pushed back on writing our own TLS, the condition was: test it like we didn't trust it. So every "it works" is checked against someone else's tests: Wycheproof, the RFCs, and the suites of npm, pnpm, yarn and bun.
story.p3: The numbers decide. An HTTP/2 client was built, benchmarked on GitHub's runners and a desktop, found slower and hungrier for CPU, and deleted.
story.quote: Is jpm perfect? No. Perfect doesn't exist. There's good enough, there's great, and there's tested enough to know which one you have.
story.cta: Try jpm in your CI. Then go build the thing you didn't think you had time for.
